title: Peacemaking and Its Consequences — The Treaty of Versailles and the Fourteen Points, 1918–1919

documents.citation: President Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points Address to Congress, January 8, 1918 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain (Points I, V, XIV selected)
documents.excerpt: I. Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind... V. A free, open-minded, and absolutely impartial adjustment of all colonial claims... XIV. A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike.

documents.citation: Treaty of Versailles, Article 231 ('War Guilt Clause'), June 28, 1919 — Avalon Project, Yale Law School, public domain
documents.excerpt: Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.

documents.citation: Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, Speech on the Treaty of Versailles and Article X of the League Covenant, August 12, 1919 — Bryan, William Jennings, ed., Republic or Empire (1899), public domain, public domain
documents.excerpt: I have always loved but one flag... but I have loved America with an undivided heart, and I cannot share that devotion, cannot give affection to the mongrel banner invented for a league... I have loved but one flag and I am not prepared to put American boys under the command of some foreign general, or to bind America to go to war at the behest of other nations without the consent of Congress... Article X I consider the most dangerous obligation that has ever been submitted to the Senate.
